definition:
The doctrine of the Trinity is the church's confession that there is one God, and that this one God is the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit: three persons, each fully and equally God, who are not three gods but one. The persons are not parts of God, as if each held a third of the divine being, and they are not three roles or masks worn in turn by a single actor. The Father is God, the Son is God, and the Spirit is God; the Father is not the Son, the Son is not the Spirit, and the Spirit is not the Father; and there is one God. The word Trinity is not in the Bible. It is the church's name for a pattern it found throughout the New Testament and saw foreshadowed in the Old: the Father sends the Son, the Son makes the Father known and gives his life, and the Spirit, sent from the Father through the Son, unites believers to Christ and brings them to the Father. The study of who God is treats the confession of one God, and the studies of the incarnation and the Holy Spirit take up the Son and the Spirit in their own right; this study traces how Scripture discloses the three as the one God.

Most of the technical vocabulary came from later reflection, but it was built to guard biblical words. The Shema's 'echad, ‘one’ (Deuteronomy 6:4), is the ordinary Hebrew numeral. Some have argued that because it can describe a unity of several (a husband and wife become ‘one flesh’ in Genesis 2:24) it hints at plurality in God, but the word cannot carry that weight by itself, and the doctrine does not rest on it. The Greek trias, ‘triad’, first appears for God in Theophilus of Antioch around 180, and the Latin trinitas in Tertullian of Carthage early in the third century. The fourth-century church settled on ousia, ‘being’ or ‘essence’, for what the three share, and hypostasis, a concrete, distinct subsistence, for what each is; the Latin West spoke of one substantia and three personae. The key word of the Nicene Creed is homoousios, ‘of the same being’, said of the Son in relation to the Father. In the classical doctrine the persons are distinguished only by their relations of origin: the Father is unbegotten, the Son is eternally begotten of the Father, and the Spirit eternally proceeds. ‘Person’ here is not simply the modern word for a separate individual with a separate mind and will; how far that modern sense applies is one of the questions still debated within the confession.
ot:
The Old Testament's first and largest contribution to the doctrine is the one God himself. Israel confessed, “Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God, the LORD is One” (Deuteronomy 6:4), and heard the LORD say through Isaiah, “I am the first and I am the last, and there is no God but Me” (Isaiah 44:6). Christians have never treated this as a rival to the Trinity to be qualified away. It is the frame within which the doctrine is confessed, and the reason the church rejected every account that made Father, Son, and Spirit into three gods. Yet within that frame the Old Testament speaks of God in ways that later readers found could not be flattened. Creation itself comes by God's word and Spirit: “the Spirit of God was hovering over the surface of the waters” and “God said, ‘Let there be light’” (Genesis 1:2-3), and a psalmist sings that “By the word of the LORD the heavens were made, and all the stars by the breath of His mouth” (Psalm 33:6). God also speaks in the plural: “Let Us make man in Our image” (Genesis 1:26; compare Genesis 3:22, Genesis 11:7, and Isaiah 6:8). Many church fathers heard in these plurals the Father addressing the Son and the Spirit. Many modern interpreters read them as God addressing his heavenly court, as in the scene of 1 Kings 22:19, or as a plural of deliberation. The text does not settle the question, and the doctrine does not depend on it.

More weight falls on figures who are at once the LORD and distinguished from him. The angel of the LORD speaks to Hagar, and she names “the LORD who had spoken to her” as “the God who sees me” (Genesis 16:13). God says of the angel he sends ahead of Israel, “My Name is in him” (Exodus 23:21), and Isaiah remembers that “the Angel of His Presence saved them” (Isaiah 63:9). Some fathers saw in the three visitors to Abraham at Mamre a sign of the Trinity, others saw the Son with two angels; the text says that the LORD appeared and that Abraham saw three men, two of whom are later called angels (Genesis 18:1-2; 19:1). Wisdom speaks as a person at God's side before creation in Proverbs 8, though whether this is poetic personification or more has always been debated, and the passage became a battleground when Arius read the Greek of Proverbs 8:22, ‘the Lord created me’, as proof that the Son was a creature. The Spirit of God gives life (Job 33:4; Psalm 104:30), and Isaiah speaks of Israel rebelling and grieving “His Holy Spirit” (Isaiah 63:10), language that treats the Spirit as one who can be wronged.

The promises of the coming king and servant press further. The LORD says to the king, “You are My Son; today I have become Your Father” (Psalm 2:7). A royal psalm addresses the king, “Your throne, O God, endures forever and ever” (Psalm 45:6), which Hebrews 1:8 applies to the Son. In Psalm 110:1 “The LORD said to my Lord,” a verse Jesus himself raised as a puzzle about David's son (Mark 12:35-37). Isaiah names the promised child “Mighty God” (Isaiah 9:6), and Daniel sees “One like the Son of Man” coming with the clouds to the Ancient of Days to receive an everlasting kingdom (Daniel 7:13-14). The Spirit rests on this figure: “The Spirit of the LORD will rest on Him” (Isaiah 11:2), and the servant says, “The Spirit of the Lord GOD is on Me, because the LORD has anointed Me” (Isaiah 61:1). The prophets also promise that God will put his own Spirit within his people (Ezekiel 36:27) and pour it out on all flesh (Joel 2:28).

None of this amounts to a revealed doctrine of the Trinity in the Old Testament, and Jewish readers have read every one of these texts without it. Christians read them back in the light of Christ and the Spirit, as the New Testament authors themselves did. What the Old Testament supplies is the one God, a God who acts in the world through his Word, his Spirit, his Wisdom, and his angel without ceasing to be one, and a set of promises that God would come himself.
nt:
The New Testament contains no formula of the Trinity, but it shows the three acting together at the turning points of the story. At the annunciation, “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you,” and the child will be called “the Son of God” (Luke 1:35). At Jesus' baptism the Spirit descends on him like a dove and the Father's voice says, “You are My beloved Son” (Mark 1:10-11; Matthew 3:16-17). At the end of Matthew the risen Jesus sends the apostles to baptize “in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 28:19). The word ‘name’ is singular in Greek, and the three stand together as the one name into which a disciple is baptized.

The New Testament places the Son on the Creator's side of the line between God and everything else. John opens, “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1:1), and adds that “Through Him all things were made” (John 1:3). The Word is distinct from God (with God) and is God. In John 1:18 the oldest Greek manuscripts read ‘the one and only God’ where later ones read ‘the one and only Son’, and the BSB combines the sense: “the one and only Son, who is Himself God.” The Greek monogenēs, long rendered ‘only begotten’, is now generally understood to mean ‘one of a kind’, ‘unique’; the church's doctrine of eternal begetting does not stand or fall with the word's derivation. Jesus' opponents understood him to be “making Himself equal with God” (John 5:18). He said, “before Abraham was born, I am” (John 8:58) and “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30), and Thomas confessed him, “My Lord and my God” (John 20:28). Paul rewrote the Shema around Jesus, “one God, the Father” and “one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom all things came” (1 Corinthians 8:6), and applied Isaiah 45:23, where every knee bows to the one God, to Jesus (Philippians 2:10-11). The Son is “the image of the invisible God” through whom all things were created (Colossians 1:15-16), in whom “all the fullness of the Deity dwells in bodily form” (Colossians 2:9), and “the exact representation of His nature” (Hebrews 1:3). Romans 9:5 and Titus 2:13 probably call Jesus God as well, though in each case the punctuation or grammar of the Greek has been read in more than one way.

The Son is also truly distinct from the Father. He prays to him, speaks of “the glory I had with You before the world existed” (John 17:5), and says the Father loved him “before the foundation of the world” (John 17:24). He says, “the Father is greater than I” (John 14:28), and that the Son does not know the day or hour (Mark 13:32). The church has read these sayings in the light of the incarnation: the eternal Son speaks as the one who has taken the form of a servant (Philippians 2:6-7), and he speaks as the Son who receives all he has from the Father (John 5:26). How far these texts also show an eternal order within God is one of the questions still debated.

The Spirit, too, is personal and divine. Jesus promises “another Advocate,” the Greek paraklētos, one called alongside to help or plead, who will teach, remind, testify, and guide (John 14:16-17, 26; 15:26; 16:13-15). The word pneuma, ‘spirit’, is neuter in Greek, and some have argued from the masculine pronoun ekeinos, ‘he’, in John 16:13 that John insists on the Spirit's personhood. The pronoun may simply agree with the masculine paraklētos, so the argument is weaker than it is often made; the stronger evidence is what the Spirit does, since he hears, speaks, and glorifies Christ. The Spirit “proceeds from the Father” (John 15:26), the phrase the creed would adopt. Peter tells Ananias that lying to the Holy Spirit is lying “to God” (Acts 5:3-4), and Paul says that only the Spirit of God knows “the deep things of God” (1 Corinthians 2:10-11).

The apostles' prayers and blessings fall again and again into the threefold pattern. “The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with all of you” (2 Corinthians 13:14). There are gifts from the same Spirit, ministries from the same Lord, and workings from the same God (1 Corinthians 12:4-6). God sent his Son to redeem, then “sent the Spirit of His Son into our hearts, crying out, ‘Abba, Father!’” (Galatians 4:4-6). “Through Him we both have access to the Father by one Spirit” (Ephesians 2:18; compare Ephesians 1:3-14, Ephesians 4:4-6, 1 Peter 1:2, and Jude 20-21). Revelation shows every creature praising “Him who sits on the throne and to the Lamb” (Revelation 5:13). One well-known verse is not part of this evidence: the words about the Father, the Word, and the Spirit being three that bear witness in heaven, added to 1 John 5:7 in the King James Version, are absent from all early Greek manuscripts and entered the Greek printed text only in the sixteenth century. Modern translations, including the BSB, rightly omit them. The doctrine never needed them.

keyTexts.why: God speaks in the plural, “Let Us make man in Our image.” Many fathers read it as the Father speaking with the Son and Spirit; many modern interpreters hear God addressing his heavenly court.
The Shema confesses that the LORD is one. The doctrine of the Trinity is confessed within this frame, never against it.
The LORD speaks to David's Lord. Jesus pressed the verse as a question about who the Messiah is, and the New Testament quotes and echoes it more than almost any other Old Testament verse.
The Angel of his presence saves Israel, and Israel grieves his Holy Spirit. The Old Testament speaks of God acting through figures who are both God's own and distinct.
At Jesus' baptism the Spirit descends and the Father speaks to the Son. The three are present together at the start of Jesus' ministry.
Disciples are baptized into the one name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. The closest the Gospels come to a formula.
The Word was with God and was God, made all things, and became flesh. The Son is distinct from the Father and fully divine.
Jesus promises another Advocate, the Spirit of truth, who will dwell in the disciples. The Spirit is personal and is sent as Jesus was sent.
The Spirit proceeds from the Father and is sent by the Son. The source of the creed's language and of the later dispute over the filioque.
Lying to the Holy Spirit is lying to God. An early and plain identification of the Spirit as God.
Paul restates the Shema with one God, the Father, and one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom all things came.
The grace of the Lord Jesus, the love of God, and the fellowship of the Spirit. The apostles blessed the churches in the threefold name.
The Father sends the Son to redeem and the Spirit of the Son to make believers children who cry Abba. Salvation has a triune shape.
The one in the form of God took the form of a servant, and every knee will bow to him. Paul applies Isaiah 45:23, spoken of the one God, to Jesus.
The Son made the universe, is the radiance of God's glory and the exact representation of his nature, and upholds all things.

history:
The earliest Christians worshiped the Trinity before they explained it. They baptized in the threefold name, as the Didache (late first or early second century) directs, and around 112 the Roman governor Pliny the Younger reported to the emperor Trajan that Christians in Bithynia sang hymns to Christ as to a god. Irenaeus of Lyon, writing around 180, summarized the church's rule of faith in one God the Father, one Christ Jesus the Son, and the Holy Spirit, and pictured the Son and the Spirit as the Father's two hands in creation and salvation. The first sustained challenge came from modalism, taught by Noetus of Smyrna and by Praxeas and later associated with Sabellius in Rome, which made Father, Son, and Spirit successive modes of one person. Tertullian's Against Praxeas (around 213) answered with the formula of one substance in three persons. Origen of Alexandria (died around 253) taught that the Son is eternally begotten, never having had a beginning, though some of his language ranked the Son below the Father.

The decisive crisis began around 318, when Arius, a presbyter in Alexandria, taught that the Son was the first and greatest of God's creatures, that there was a time when he did not exist. The Council of Nicaea, called by the emperor Constantine in 325, confessed that the Son is begotten of the Father and not made, homoousios with the Father. Decades of dispute followed, and several councils and emperors favored compromise formulas. Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria from 328 to 373 and exiled five times, argued that only one who is truly God can save and that the church already worshiped the Son. The Cappadocians, Basil of Caesarea, Gregory of Nazianzus, and Gregory of Nyssa, clarified the terms (one ousia, three hypostaseis) and defended the full deity of the Spirit against those called Pneumatomachians, ‘Spirit-fighters’; Basil's On the Holy Spirit dates from about 375 and Gregory of Nazianzus's Theological Orations from 380. The Council of Constantinople in 381 reaffirmed Nicaea and expanded the creed to confess the Spirit as the Lord and giver of life, who proceeds from the Father and is worshiped and glorified together with the Father and the Son. Both East and West taught that the works of God toward the world are undivided: the three act inseparably, each in his own way.

In the West, Augustine's On the Trinity (written over roughly two decades, around 400 to 420) explored the doctrine through Scripture and through analogies in the human mind, such as memory, understanding, and will. The Athanasian Creed, a Latin statement from the fifth or sixth century not written by Athanasius, set out the Western confession in careful balance. The Latin church came to say that the Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son (filioque); the phrase was added to the creed in Spain, notably at the Third Council of Toledo in 589, spread in the Frankish church, and was adopted in the liturgy at Rome early in the eleventh century. The Greek church objected both to the addition and to its theology, most sharply under Patriarch Photius in the ninth century, and the dispute became one of the causes of the separation of East and West usually dated to 1054. Reunion was attempted at the councils of Lyon (1274) and Florence (1439) without lasting success. John of Damascus in the eighth century gave classic form to the idea of perichoresis, the mutual indwelling of the persons, and Thomas Aquinas in the thirteenth century described the persons as subsisting relations.

The Reformers received the ancient creeds without change. Michael Servetus was executed in Geneva in 1553 for, among other things, denying the Trinity, and the Socinians of Poland set out a unitarian faith in the Racovian Catechism (1605). The Protestant confessions, among them the Belgic Confession (1561), the Thirty-Nine Articles (1563), and the Westminster Confession (1646), confessed the Trinity in the Nicene terms. In the modern period Friedrich Schleiermacher placed the doctrine at the end of The Christian Faith (1821 to 1822), while Karl Barth opened his Church Dogmatics (first volume 1932) with it as the doctrine of revelation itself. Karl Rahner's The Trinity (1967) argued that the Trinity revealed in the history of salvation is the Trinity as God eternally is, and the reverse. Jürgen Moltmann (The Trinity and the Kingdom, 1980) and John Zizioulas (Being as Communion, 1985) developed accounts centered on communion among the persons, and in the early twenty-first century historians such as Lewis Ayres (Nicaea and Its Legacy, 2004) led a retrieval of the fourth-century theology. The site's full treatment at /theology/doctrine/trinity surveys the one live evangelical debate, over eternal subordination, at length.

differ.body: The Spirit eternally proceeds from the Father and the Son as from one principle. Defenders in the Catholic and most Protestant traditions, following Augustine, argue that the Spirit is called both “the Spirit of God” and “the Spirit of Christ” (Romans 8:9), that the Son sends the Spirit (John 15:26; 16:7), and that the Spirit takes what is the Son's because all that the Father has belongs to the Son (John 16:14-15). If the Son shares everything with the Father except being Father, he shares in the Spirit's procession too. Many Western theologians grant that the clause was added to the creed without an ecumenical council, and some have proposed restoring the original wording while keeping the theology.

The Spirit eternally proceeds from the Father alone, who is the one source within the Godhead, and is sent into the world by the Son in time. Orthodox theologians argue that John 15:26 speaks of procession from the Father and of sending by the Son, and that the West confused the Spirit's eternal origin with his mission. They hold that a single source preserves the Father's unique role and guards against blurring the persons, and that no part of the church had authority to alter a creed agreed by an ecumenical council. Some Eastern writers accept that the Spirit proceeds from the Father through the Son, a phrase with roots in Greek fathers, as a meeting point.

Classical theologians, retrieving Augustine, the Cappadocians, and Aquinas, stress that God has one mind, one will, and one power, and that the persons are distinguished only by their relations of origin; the three act inseparably in every work. Social trinitarians, among them Moltmann, Zizioulas, and a number of analytic philosophers, stress the Bible's portrait of Father and Son loving, speaking, and sending each other, and describe the persons as distinct centers of knowing and loving united in perfect communion. Each side holds the Nicene confession and warns of a danger in the other: classical writers see a drift toward three gods, social writers see a drift toward a single person with three names. The debate turns partly on what the word ‘person’ should mean.

Some evangelical theologians, notably Wayne Grudem and Bruce Ware, hold that the Son, equal to the Father in being, eternally relates to him in a role of glad submission, and they cite texts such as 1 Corinthians 11:3 and 1 Corinthians 15:28. Others, including Kevin Giles, Fred Sanders, and many confessional Reformed and Catholic writers, hold that the one divine will and authority belong equally to all three, that the order among the persons is one of origin, not command, and that the Son's obedience belongs to his mission as the incarnate servant (Philippians 2:6-8). Both confess the Son's full deity. The site's Trinity page gives each view at length.

errors:
The creeds were written against specific errors, and each is still met today. Modalism, associated with Sabellius, says that one divine person appears successively as Father, Son, and Spirit, like one actor wearing three masks; it cannot account for the Son praying to the Father or the Father speaking to the Son at the baptism. The same view reappeared in the early twentieth century in Oneness Pentecostalism. Arianism made the Son the first and highest creature, and its modern heirs, including the Jehovah's Witnesses, still read Proverbs 8:22 and Colossians 1:15 that way. The church rejected it because it puts a creature on the throne and leaves salvation in the hands of someone who is not God. Adoptionism, taught by Theodotus in Rome around 190 and by Paul of Samosata, who was condemned at Antioch in 268, held that Jesus was a man adopted as God's Son. The Pneumatomachians, who denied the Spirit's deity, were answered at Constantinople in 381. Tritheism, the belief in three gods, is the opposite error; it was charged against John Philoponus in the sixth century and denies the Shema.

The common illustrations for the Trinity often fall into the same errors. Water as ice, liquid, and steam is modalism, since one substance takes three forms in turn. An egg with shell, white, and yolk makes each person a part of God. A man who is father, son, and husband is again one person in three roles. The church's own practice has been more restrained: it confesses what Scripture reveals, guards it with careful words, and admits that no created thing is a full picture of the Creator.
life:
The Trinity is not a puzzle to be solved before a person can pray. It is the shape of Christian prayer and life. Believers pray to the Father, through the Son, in the Spirit (Ephesians 2:18); they are baptized into the name of the three; and they are blessed at the end of worship in the same name. The doctrine means that God's love did not begin when he made the world. Before creation the Father loved the Son (John 17:24), so love is not something God acquired or needed from creatures, and his love for them is a free gift out of a fullness that was always there.

It also means that God himself comes near. The Son who reveals the Father is not a messenger standing outside God, and the Spirit who lives in believers is not a substitute for God's presence. Jesus prayed that his followers would be one “as You, Father, are in Me, and I am in You” (John 17:21), and Christians have taken the unity of the Father and the Son as the pattern and ground of the church's own life. Their hope is to share, as creatures and by grace, in the life of the God who has always been Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.
questions: The first Christians were Jews who confessed the Shema daily. Which New Testament texts show them including Jesus and the Spirit within the one God without abandoning that confession?
Why did the church at Nicaea and Constantinople think it mattered for salvation that the Son and the Spirit are fully God and not the highest creatures?

Common illustrations of the Trinity (water, an egg, one man in three roles) each fall into an old error. Why do you think the doctrine resists illustration, and what does that suggest about knowing God?
